opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, when I first got to know their work, I saw them mainly as extremely strong engineers. Progressive GAN came out and the results were stunning, and my first reaction, like a lot of people in the community, was: okay, they must have a lot of compute and they're very good at tuning. I think I underestimated what was really going on.

As I worked more closely with them at NVIDIA, my view changed quite a bit. What impressed me most was their discipline. In the GAN field at the time, many of us, including myself, were in a mode of proposing a new loss, a new architecture, getting a better number, and writing the paper. Tero, Timo, and Samuli didn't work like that. They would stay on one problem for a very long time and keep asking: why does this artifact appear? Why is this image slightly wrong? They looked at the generated images with an almost obsessive level of care, the way a graphics person looks at a render. That comes from their background in computer graphics, where if something is a little bit off, the human eye catches it immediately, and you're not allowed to say "the metric is fine."

Their papers also looked simple on the surface, but every component had been tested, removed, put back, and understood. Things like the style-based generator or the later fixes for aliasing weren't tricks. They came from really understanding the signal processing and the failure modes. I came to see their approach as more scientific than I first thought, almost the opposite of the "throw ideas at the wall" culture.

It also changed how I run my own research. I learned that quality is a goal in itself, that it's worth spending a year to make something genuinely work instead of six papers that each work a little. And they cared deeply about releasing clean code and models so others could build on them, which is a big part of why StyleGAN had so much impact. So my view went from "these are great engineers" to "these are people with a very clear research taste and the patience to follow it," and that's much rarer.

r001.rationale: He says he underestimated what was going on, not that he initially thought the researchers underestimated the difficulty of GAN research.

r002.rationale: He describes sustained work on problems and mentions StyleGAN and later aliasing fixes, but does not identify investment across successive StyleGAN generations.

r003.rationale: He says their careful, disciplined approach changed how he runs his own research and taught him to prioritize quality and spend longer making work succeed.

fable-5.1.text:
When I first joined NVIDIA Research, I was coming from a different world. In those days, most of us doing generative models were thinking about the problem in a very machine learning way: define a loss, think about the theory, run experiments on the standard benchmarks, write the paper. That was the culture I knew.

Tero, Timo, and Samuli came from graphics. Their background was real-time rendering, ray tracing, that kind of thing. And honestly, in the beginning, I did not fully understand how they worked. They were very slow in a certain sense. They would spend weeks, even months, on something that looked to me like an engineering detail. Why is the network producing this artifact? Why does the image get worse when you change this normalization? They would just stare at the samples, build visualization tools, and keep digging until they truly understood the behavior. There was no rush to publish. At that time I thought, this is a bit too much, we should be moving faster.

But then Progressive GAN came out, and then StyleGAN, and I realized what I had been missing. Their approach was not about adding a clever new loss or a new theory. It was about caring deeply about the quality of the output, almost like an artist or a craftsman, and then being extremely rigorous and honest in the experiments. Every design choice was tested in isolation. Nothing was left to superstition. That is actually a very graphics mindset: in rendering, if a pixel is wrong, it is wrong, and you have to find out why. They brought that discipline to GANs, and it turned out that was exactly what the field needed. GAN training was full of folklore, and they replaced the folklore with understanding.

So my view changed from "they are too slow" to "they are doing the real work." I learned from them that engineering excellence is research. The details are not beneath the science; the details are the science. And I learned patience, that if you let a small team go deep on one problem for a long time without pressure, you can get something much more impactful than ten quick papers.

The other thing I came to appreciate was how humble they were. Tero in particular would never claim more than what the experiments showed. That kind of honesty built a lot of trust, inside NVIDIA and in the community. When StyleGAN came out, people believed the results immediately, because everyone knew these were people who do not exaggerate. I try to carry that into my own group now.

r001.rationale: He initially thought they were moving too slowly and focusing too much on engineering details; he does not say they underestimated how difficult GAN research was.

r002.rationale: He mentions Progressive GAN and StyleGAN, but does not describe sustained investment across successive StyleGAN generations.

r003.rationale: He says he learned from their detailed, rigorous approach and carries their honesty and discipline into his own group.

astra-6.text:
As I worked with Tero, Timo, and Samuli, I came to appreciate that their strength wasn’t just in coming up with clever ideas. It was in how carefully they examined those ideas. You could have a promising result, but then the question was: Why does it work? What experiment would tell us whether our explanation is actually right?

That shifted my emphasis from finding a technique that improves the result to understanding what produces the improvement. With GANs, where so many things interact, that discipline matters a lot. I came to see their approach as a combination of creativity and a very high standard for evidence.

r001.rationale: The candidate does not say Ming-Yu initially thought they underestimated the difficulty of GAN research.

r002.rationale: The candidate does not mention sustained investment across successive StyleGAN generations.

r003.rationale: The candidate says their careful examination of ideas shifted his own emphasis toward understanding what causes improvements and demanding strong evidence.

sol-6.1.text:
What I came to appreciate was how much care went into testing an idea. At first, you see the results and think, “They must have some really clever trick.” But working with them, I came to see the process as the important part: question the assumptions, build a strong baseline, and run experiments that help you understand what is actually making a difference.

That changed my own perspective. A surprising result is a starting point. The next question is, “Why does this work, and can we isolate the reason?” That discipline was what I really learned to appreciate.

r001.rationale: The response describes initially expecting a clever trick, but does not say Liu thought they underestimated the difficulty of GAN research.

r002.rationale: It does not mention sustained investment across successive StyleGAN generations.

r003.rationale: The response says their process changed Liu’s perspective and that he learned to appreciate it, but does not clearly state that their attention to detail influenced his own research approach.
